--------
Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev joins DJ Vlad to discuss how commission-free trading changed the investing landscape after Robinhood opened to the public in 2015. DJ Vlad, a self-described Warren Buffett-style buy-and-hold investor, explains why removing trading fees — and later adding fractional shares — made active stock trading feel closer to gambling than long-term investing, citing examples like Google, Amazon, Instagram, YouTube, and Bitcoin-style market access.

Tenev acknowledges that lower barriers can make it easier for users to act against their own strategies, while emphasizing Robinhood’s mission to give people more control over their money. The conversation also covers passive investing, indexing, risk management, and Robinhood’s new 24/7 stock trading feature in the U.S., including the debate over whether weekend stock access adds danger or helps investors respond to breaking company news. A candid look at trading risk, financial freedom, and modern retail investing.

--------
Dale Comstock pushes back hard on Robert O’Neill’s claim on VladTV that an “unspoken rule” allowed up to 23 civilian casualties while targeting one terrorist. Speaking with Vlad, Comstock says there is no acceptable number of innocent deaths in combat, calling the idea irresponsible and damaging to the public’s understanding of military operations. He explains that missions in Afghanistan required precision planning, not a “collateral damage” mindset, and shares a painful battlefield story involving Taliban attacks, an observation post, Afghan civilians, and the lasting moral weight of unintended casualties. Comstock also opens up about PTSD, remorse, and the difference between accepting the realities of war and treating civilian loss as permissible. The conversation touches on Navy SEAL culture, Osama bin Laden raid veteran Robert O’Neill, rules of engagement, counterterrorism, Afghanistan warfare, and the human cost behind today’s military debates.

--------
Vincent “Gigi” Marino sits down with Vlad to reflect on receiving a 35-year prison sentence at age 35, the psychological weight of facing decades behind bars, and why he says cooperation was never an option. Marino discusses the judge’s remark about his future parole officer not yet being born, the 25-year sentencing enhancement he claims was added despite a jury finding, and references to George Orwell’s 1984, Minority Report, and “reasonable foreseeability” in his case. He also breaks down how authorities connected him to a Massachusetts killing through a prison phone book containing his personal information, while later accounts pointed to mistaken identity involving a state trooper and a young victim. After serving 28 years behind the wall—and nearly 29 years and six months including BOP halfway house and home detention—Marino explains his fight for freedom and refusal to cooperate.

In this VladTV interview, Charleston White addresses the viral clip from a Fort Worth political debate held inside a church, where Mayor Mattie Parker faced Deborah Peoples. White says the setting became a political arena—not a worship service—arguing that church and state should remain separate. He explains why he reacted angrily after a woman allegedly approached him from behind, made noise, and sat beside him while others laughed and recorded.

White gives his account of calling the woman a “nappy-headed b****,” saying he felt ambushed and didn’t realize the incident was being filmed. He also reflects on cursing inside the church, comments he made about God, and why he now feels the public never heard the full story behind the viral moment. A candid discussion on politics, religion, public backlash, and Charleston White’s unfiltered response.

--------
Former Army Ranger sniper Nicholas Irving joins Shawn Prez for a frank discussion on modern war, U.S. foreign policy, and the myth of fighting “for freedom.” Irving breaks down why controlling the Strait of Hormuz, confronting Iran, and battling groups like the Houthis is far more complicated than destroying a navy, drawing from his experiences in Iraq and Afghanistan. The conversation revisits weapons of mass destruction claims under George W. Bush, Saddam Hussein, Vietnam’s 58,220 American deaths, Trump’s hardline rhetoric, oil politics involving Venezuela, and questions around Jared Kushner’s Middle East business ties.

Irving argues that today’s wars are driven by profit, politics, confusion, and personal survival—not patriotic slogans. He also explains why elite military culture, from Rangers to SEAL Team Six and Delta Force, is fueled by ego, ambition, and loyalty to the person beside you rather than abstract ideas of America.
